10.1111/apt.12913.results_passage: Four trials met the inclusion criteria, one in constipation and three in non-constipated subjects. In constipation, 3 weeks of prune consumption (100 g/day) improved stool frequency (3.5 vs. 2.8 CSBM per week, P = 0.006) and stool consistency (3.2 vs. 2.8 on Bristol stool form scale, P = 0.02) compared with psyllium (22 g/day). In non-constipated subjects, prunes softened stool consistency in one trial and increased stool weight (628 g vs. 514 g/72 h wet weight, P = 0.001) in another trial, compared with control. In constipation, prunes appear superior to psyllium for improving stool frequency and consistency, however, the evidence for other outcomes and the effects in non-constipated subjects is weak.

10.6133/apjcn.2015.24.3.15.results_passage: There was no difference in total bowel movements over 3 weeks (p>0.05) or mean bowel movements during each of weeks 1, 2 and 3 (p>0.05) between the kiwifruit extract and placebo when assessed from a faecal diary. There was also no detectable difference in defecation related scores of ease of defecation, volume, consistency or stool type assessed using Bristol stool chart scores. Nor was there a significant change in gastrointestinal symptoms rating scale or quality of life between pre and post treatment measures, compared to placebo (p>0.05). This trial showed that improvement in bowel function or comfort was not achieved through supplementation with 1 g/day freeze dried kiwifruit extract.

10.1097/MCG.0b013e3182a88357.results_passage: Nine studies that evaluated 726 patients were identified. Peppermint oil was found to be significantly superior to placebo for global improvement of IBS symptoms (5 studies, 392 patients, relative risk 2.23; 95% confidence interval, 1.78-2.81) and improvement in abdominal pain (5 studies, 357 patients, relative risk 2.14; 95% confidence interval, 1.64-2.79). Although peppermint oil patients were significantly more likely to experience an adverse event, such events were mild and transient in nature. Peppermint oil is a safe and effective short-term treatment for IBS.

10.1016/j.clnesp.2024.02.025.results_passage: A total of 20 studies involving 3011 patients were obtained. The results demonstrated that probiotics are more effective than placebo in reducing global IBS symptoms improvement rate (RR = 1.401, 95% CI 1.182-1.662, P < 0.001) and quality of life scores (SMD = 0.286, 95% CI = 0.154-0.418, P < 0.001). High doses (daily dose of probiotics >= 10^10) or multiple strains of probiotics exhibit beneficial effects on abdominal pain. Probiotics are effective and safe for IBS patients, though high heterogeneity makes definite conclusions challenging.

10.1016/j.nut.2017.07.004.results_passage: Nine RCTs with a total of 596 subjects were included. A meta-analysis revealed significant group differences for the low FODMAP diet compared with other diets with regard to gastrointestinal symptoms (SMD = -0.62; 95% CI = -0.93 to -0.31; P = 0.0001), abdominal pain (SMD = -0.50; 95% CI = -0.77 to -0.22; P = 0.008), and health-related quality of life (SMD = 0.36; 95% CI = 0.10-0.62; P = 0.007). This meta-analysis found evidence of the short-term efficacy and safety of the low FODMAP diet in patients with IBS, though only a preliminary recommendation can be made until long-term effects are investigated.

10.1055/s-2008-1038600.results_passage: Analyses revealed no differences in quality of life scores between groups at 12-week follow-up. The exercise group reported significantly improved symptoms of constipation (mean difference=10.9, 95% CI= -20.1, -1.6) compared to usual care at follow-up. The intervention group participated in significantly more exercise than usual care at follow-up (mean difference=21.6, 95% CI=9.4, 33.8). Findings highlight the possibility that exercise may be an effective intervention for symptom management in patients with irritable bowel syndrome, particularly for constipation predominant patients.

10.1159/000050681.results_passage: The available data clearly demonstrate that inhibition of gastric emptying and stimulation of colonic transit is the most consistent pattern in the motility response of the gastrointestinal tract to acute or short-term stress. The colonic motor response to stress is exaggerated in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), with an increased emotional response associated with this difference in colonic and gastric motor responses to certain stressors. Endogenous corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) in the brain plays a significant role in mediating stress-induced inhibition of upper GI and stimulation of lower GI motor function. Stress-induced activation of mucosal mast cells in the GI tract also appears to be involved in stress-associated alterations of visceral sensitivity.

10.1038/ajg.2016.503.results_passage: A total of 101 adolescents with IBS (13-17 years of age) were included in this study, with low dropout rates (6%). Analyses showed a significantly larger pretreatment to posttreatment change on the primary outcome, Gastrointestinal Symptoms Rating Scale for IBS (B=-6.42, P=0.006, effect size Cohen's d=0.45, 95% CI 0.12-0.77), for the Internet-delivered CBT group compared with the wait-list control group. After 6 months, the results were stable or significantly improved. Internet-delivered CBT based on exposure exercises for adolescents with IBS can effectively improve gastrointestinal symptoms and quality of life.

10.1097/00042737-199802000-00003.results_passage: Caffeinated coffee, decaffeinated coffee and a meal induced more activity in the colon with a greater area under the curve of pressure waves (P < 0.01) and a greater number of propagated contractions (P < 0.05) compared with water. The effects of decaffeinated coffee on colonic motility were not significantly different from those of water or caffeinated coffee, and were lower (P < 0.05) than those of a meal. Caffeinated coffee stimulates colonic motor activity, with a magnitude similar to a meal, 60% stronger than water, and 23% stronger than decaffeinated coffee.

10.1080/13697137.2022.2097865.results_passage: Across 21 RCTs involving 2884 participants, compared to no-treatment control, exercise significantly improved severity of vasomotor symptoms (10 studies, standardized mean difference [SMD] = 0.25; 95% CI: 0.04 to 0.47, p = 0.02, very low certainty of evidence); the effect size was attenuated when studies with a high risk of bias were excluded (SMD = 0.11, 95% CI: -0.03 to 0.26, p = 0.13). No significant changes in vasomotor frequency were found between exercise and control (SMD = 0.14, 95% CI: -0.03 to 0.31, p = 0.12, high certainty of evidence). Exercise might improve vasomotor symptom severity, but future rigorous RCTs are warranted to explore optimal exercise prescription.

10.1017/S0033291721005407.results_passage: 14 RCTs comprising 1618 patients with a mean sample size of 116 were included. Cognitive therapy and behavior therapy (CTBT) significantly outperformed control groups in terms of reducing hot flushes (g = 0.39, 95% CI 0.23-0.55), night sweats, depression (g = 0.50, 95% CI 0.34-0.66), anxiety (g = 0.38, 95% CI 0.23-0.54), fatigue, and quality of life. CTBT is an effective psychological treatment for menopausal symptoms, with predominantly small to moderate effects that are sustained long-term, although the efficacy declines somewhat over time and was stronger for natural menopause symptoms than treatment-induced menopause symptoms.

10.1097/gme.0b013e3182410159.results_passage: From 277 potentially relevant publications, 19 trials were included in the systematic review and 17 trials were selected for meta-analyses. Ingestion of soy isoflavones (median, 54 mg aglycone equivalents) for 6 weeks to 12 months significantly reduced the frequency of hot flashes by 20.6% (95% CI, -28.38 to -12.86; P < 0.00001) compared with placebo. Isoflavones also significantly reduced hot flash severity by 26.2% (95% CI: -42.23 to -10.15, P = 0.001) compared with placebo. Soy isoflavone supplements, derived by extraction or chemical synthesis, are significantly more effective than placebo in reducing the frequency and severity of hot flashes.

10.1177/0022034516655315.results_passage: Of 5,494 titles retrieved, 33 studies were eligible for inclusion. Self-reported infrequent brushers demonstrated higher incidence (odds ratio [OR], 1.50; 95% CI, 1.34 to 1.69) and increment (standardized mean difference [SMD], 0.28; 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.44) of carious lesions than frequent brushers. The effect of infrequent brushing on incidence and increment of carious lesions was higher in deciduous (OR: 1.75; 95% CI: 1.49 to 2.06) than permanent dentition (OR: 1.39; 95% CI: 1.29 to 1.49). Meta-regression indicated that none of the included variables (sample size, follow-up period, diagnosis level, methodological quality) influenced the effect estimate.

10.1016/j.amepre.2018.02.014.results_passage: Twenty-eight studies were included in the review; of these, only 14 presented data that could be included in the meta-analysis. Pooled adjusted risk ratios estimate that smoking increases the risk of periodontitis by 85% (risk ratio=1.85, 95% CI=1.5, 2.2). Meta-regression demonstrated that age explained 54.2% of the variability between studies, time of follow-up explained 13.5%, loss to follow-up 10.7%, criteria used to assess periodontal status explained 2.1%, and severity of periodontitis explained 16.9%. Smoking has a detrimental effect on the incidence and progression of periodontitis.

10.1016/S2468-2667(26)00149-0.results_passage: The review screened 45,477 records and included 28 longitudinal studies from 16 countries, encompassing over 300,000 participants. Individuals with periodontitis at baseline showed an 18-25% higher occurrence of newly incident type 2 diabetes during follow-up, and baseline diabetes status was associated with a higher rate of newly incident periodontitis. Tooth loss was also associated with newly incident type 2 diabetes over time (HR 1.12-1.20), and individuals who were edentulous at baseline showed a higher occurrence of newly incident type 2 diabetes (RR 1.30). People with periodontitis and edentulism are more likely to be diagnosed with type 2 diabetes in the future, and people with diabetes are more likely to be diagnosed with periodontitis, though with less consistent evidence.

10.23950/jcmk/15827.results_passage: This systematic review and meta-analysis included six randomised controlled trials published between 2013 and 2020. According to the pooled results of the six studies, calcium reduced the severity of PMS complaints (p=0.002; I2 = 76.2%) when calcium administration was compared with the control group for the reduction of PMS complaints. On the other hand, the severity of PMS complaints did not change when calcium administration was compared with other treatments (p=0.416; I2 = 54.7%). This study showed that calcium effectively reduced the severity of PMS complaints compared to the control groups.

10.1002/art.41416.license: NIH-funded author manuscript (not a CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/art.41416.results_passage: We included 1,398 participants who returned at least one knee pain questionnaire. Mean age was 67.7 years, 66% were female, and mean WOMAC Pain was 37 (SD 19). WOMAC Pain did not differ between vitamin D or marine omega-3 fatty acid supplementation and placebo at any time point during follow-up (linear time by treatment interactions were not statistically significant; vitamin D p=0.41, omega-3 p=0.77). Vitamin D and omega-3 fatty acid supplementation for a mean of 5.3 years did not reduce knee pain or improve function or stiffness in a large sample of U.S. adults with chronic knee pain.

10.1186/s13018-023-04182-w.results_passage: Four trials involving 507 patients with knee osteoarthritis were included and analyzed using the random-effects model, though all trials were considered to have a high risk of bias. Results revealed a significant difference in pain relief between the collagen peptide group and the placebo group (standardized mean difference: -0.58; 95% CI -0.98, -0.18, p=0.004; I2: 68%; quality of evidence: moderate). There was no significant difference in the risk of adverse events between collagen peptide and placebo (odds ratio: 1.66; 95% CI 0.99, 2.78, p=0.05). Findings demonstrate significant pain relief in patients with knee osteoarthritis who received collagen peptides compared to placebo, though well-designed randomized controlled trials are needed to validate these findings.

10.1093/ajcn/nqac184.results_passage: Sixteen RCTs with 1251 participants were included. Overall, 311 of 473 (66%) participants responded to fiber treatment versus 134 of 329 (41%) with control treatment (RR: 1.48; 95% CI: 1.17, 1.88; P=0.001), with psyllium and pectin having significant effects. Fiber increased stool frequency (SMD: 0.72; 95% CI: 0.36, 1.08) and improved stool consistency (SMD: 0.32; 95% CI: 0.18, 0.46), particularly with higher fiber doses (>10 g/d) and treatment durations of at least 4 weeks. Fiber supplementation is effective at improving constipation, though caution is needed when interpreting the results due to considerable heterogeneity.

10.1136/bmj.b3154.results_passage: 275 patients aged 18-65 years with irritable bowel syndrome were randomised to 12 weeks of treatment with psyllium, bran, or placebo. The proportion of responders was significantly greater in the psyllium group than in the placebo group during the first month (57% v 35%; relative risk 1.60, 95% CI 1.13 to 2.26) and the second month of treatment (59% v 41%; 1.44, 1.02 to 2.06). Bran was more effective than placebo during the third month of treatment only (57% v 32%), but this was not statistically significant in the worst case analysis. Psyllium offers benefits in patients with irritable bowel syndrome in primary care.

10.1186/1475-2891-12-78.results_passage: One hundred thirty-eight subjects reporting occasional constipation were screened and 87 were randomized to placebo (n=44) and Kivia powder (n=43). There were significant increases in spontaneous bowel movements (SBM) at week 1 through week 4 compared to baseline, with SBM demonstrating significant differences between treatment and placebo groups at week 3 (p=0.000) and week 4 (p=0.020). Complete spontaneous bowel movements (CSBM) were significantly higher for the treatment group compared to placebo at week 2 (p=0.001), and abdominal discomfort, flatulence, and bowel urgency were also significantly reduced. Treatment with Kivia powder for four weeks was well tolerated and more effective than placebo in enhancing bowel movement frequency and reducing abdominal pain and flatulence in subjects with occasional constipation.

10.3390/jcm13164934.results_passage: Eleven studies (n=323) were eligible for the systematic review, of which nine (n=286) were included in the meta-analysis. Pooled analysis revealed a statistically significant decrease in circulating CRP (SMD 0.39, 95% CI 0.22, 0.56), IL-6, TNF-alpha, androstenedione, and luteinising hormone after weight loss compared to baseline levels among PCOS women, alongside a statistically significant increase in circulating SHBG (SMD -0.43, 95% CI -0.65, -0.21). These findings suggest that weight loss induced by dietary interventions seems to improve PCOS-related chronic inflammation and hyperandrogenism, although the causative relationship between the improvement in inflammation and hyperandrogenism remains to be determined.

figures.caption: Overall CRP pooled analysis of 9 studies.
figures.shows: Forest plot of the pooled standardized mean difference in circulating CRP before versus after diet-induced weight loss across 9 studies in women with PCOS.

10.1530/EC-17-0243.results_passage: Nine RCTs involving 247 cases and 249 controls were included. Significant decreases in fasting insulin (SMD = -1.021 uU/mL, 95% CI: -1.791 to -0.251, P=0.009) and HOMA index (SMD = -0.585, 95% CI: -1.145 to -0.025, P=0.041) were identified after myo-inositol supplementation. A significant increase in serum SHBG was observed only in studies where myo-inositol was administered for at least 24 weeks (SMD = 0.425 nmol/L, 95% CI: 0.050-0.801, P=0.026). These results highlight the beneficial effect of myo-inositol in improving the metabolic profile of women with PCOS, concomitantly reducing their hyperandrogenism.

10.1038/s41598-018-34303-z.results_passage: Six RCTs met the inclusion criteria. Two RCTs found favorable effects of heat therapy on menstrual pain compared with unheated placebo therapy, three RCTs found favorable effects of heating pads on menstrual pain compared with analgesic medication (n=274; SMD -0.72; 95% CI -0.97 to -0.48; P<0.001), and one RCT showed beneficial effects of heat therapy compared with no treatment (n=132; MD -4.04 VAS; 95% CI -4.88 to -3.20; P<0.001). This review provided suggestive evidence of the effectiveness of heat therapy for primary dysmenorrhea, but rigorous high-quality trials with larger sample sizes are still needed to provide robust evidence.

10.1136/bmj.318.7195.1375.license: Copyright BMJ 1999 (pre-CC era, no open license; not reusable)
10.1136/bmj.318.7195.1375.results_passage: Nine published trials representing 940 patients with premenstrual syndrome were included. The odds ratio relative to placebo for an improvement in overall premenstrual symptoms was 2.32 (95% CI 1.95 to 2.54), and the odds ratio for improvement in depressive symptoms was 1.69 (1.39 to 2.06) from four trials representing 541 patients. Conclusions are limited by the low quality of most of the trials included. Results suggest that doses of vitamin B-6 up to 100 mg/day are likely to be of benefit in treating premenstrual symptoms and premenstrual depression, but a randomised controlled trial of sufficient power and quality is needed to establish definitive recommendations.

10.1016/j.ajog.2019.10.103.license: NIH-funded author manuscript (not a CC license; not reusable)
10.1016/j.ajog.2019.10.103.results_passage: Pooled data on 21,460 midlife women from eight studies were used for cross-sectional analysis, with four studies providing prospective data (n=11,986). Never smokers who were obese had a 1.5-fold (RRR 1.52; 95% CI 1.35-1.73) higher risk of often/severe vasomotor symptoms compared with never smokers of normal weight, and the risk was much greater among smokers who were obese (RRR 3.02; 95% CI 2.41-3.78). Smokers who quit before age 40 were at similar risk levels as never smokers, and higher body mass index was associated with increased risk of vasomotor symptoms in pre- and perimenopause but with reduced risk postmenopause. High body mass index and cigarette smoking substantially increased women's risk of frequent or severe vasomotor symptoms in a dose-response manner, and maintaining normal weight and quitting smoking before age 40 may mitigate this excess risk.

10.1016/j.heliyon.2021.e08338.results_passage: Of 935 initial publications, 8 articles were finally included, covering 412 overweight and obese individuals with PCOS. Measured emotional health (3 studies, 132 participants, SMD: -1.97; 95% CI -3.54, -0.40, P=0.01) and body hair (3 studies, 132 participants, SMD: -0.40; 95% CI -0.46, -0.35, P<0.0001) were significantly lower in women on a low glycemic index diet (LGD) versus control diet groups, while infertility (SMD: 1.45; 95% CI 0.30, 2.61, P=0.01) was significantly higher in the LGD group. The meta-analysis shows LGD may play a significant role in reducing risk and improving clinical and biochemical features of PCOS, though evidence is not yet strong enough for a definite dietary recommendation.

10.1016/j.heliyon.2023.e14291.results_passage: 13 RCTs with 840 PCOS patients were included. Meta-analyses indicated that vitamin D supplementation increased serum vitamin D level (MD=17.81, 95% CI 10.65, 24.97) and endometrial thickness (MD=1.78, 95% CI 0.49, 3.06, P=0.007), and reduced serum hs-CRP, parathyroid hormone, total cholesterol, and total testosterone level (all P<0.05). No significant differences in SHBG level or modified Ferriman-Gallwey score between vitamin D and control groups were found. Vitamin D may be helpful to improve endocrine and metabolism-related indexes in patients with PCOS, though more high-quality studies with larger sample sizes are warranted.

10.1177/0022034513508954.license: No CC license found (publisher copyright; not reusable)
10.1177/0022034513508954.results_passage: From 5,990 papers identified, 55 studies were eligible: 3 intervention, 8 cohort, 20 population, and 24 cross-sectional studies. Of these, 42 of 50 studies in children and 5 of 5 in adults reported at least one positive association between sugars intake and caries. There is evidence of moderate quality showing that caries is lower when free-sugars intake is less than 10% of energy; with a less-than-5%-of-energy cut-off, a significant relationship was observed, but the evidence was judged to be of very low quality. Data variability limited meta-analysis, but the findings are relevant to minimizing caries risk throughout the life course.

10.1002/14651858.CD003053.pub6.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD003053.pub6.results_passage: 48 studies (4451 women) were included, 42 of which investigated metformin (4024 women); evidence quality ranged from very low to moderate. Metformin may improve live birth rates compared with placebo (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.51, 4 studies, 435 women, low-quality evidence), and had higher rates of clinical pregnancy (OR 1.93, 95% CI 1.42 to 2.64) and ovulation (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.81 to 3.59), though the metformin group experienced more gastrointestinal side effects (OR 4.76, 95% CI 3.06 to 7.41). An improvement in clinical pregnancy and ovulation suggests that clomiphene citrate remains preferable to metformin for ovulation induction in obese women with PCOS, while combined metformin and clomiphene citrate therapy may be useful, although it is unclear whether this translates into increased live births.

10.1002/14651858.CD001751.pub3.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD001751.pub3.results_passage: 80 randomised controlled trials (5820 women) comparing 20 different NSAIDs versus placebo, paracetamol or each other were included. Among women with primary dysmenorrhoea, NSAIDs were more effective for pain relief than placebo (OR 4.37, 95% CI 3.76 to 5.09; 35 RCTs, low quality evidence), meaning that if 18% of women taking placebo achieve moderate or excellent pain relief, between 45% and 53% taking NSAIDs will do so. However, NSAIDs were associated with more adverse effects (overall adverse effects OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.51; gastrointestinal adverse effects OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.23). NSAIDs appear to be a very effective treatment for dysmenorrhoea, though women using them need to be aware of the substantial risk of adverse effects, and there is insufficient evidence to determine which individual NSAID is safest and most effective.

10.1002/14651858.CD004142.pub4.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD004142.pub4.results_passage: 12 trials with 854 women were included in the review, with 10 trials and 754 women in the meta-analysis; nine compared exercise with no treatment and one compared exercise with NSAIDs. Exercise may have a large effect on reducing menstrual pain intensity compared to no exercise (standardised mean difference -1.86, 95% CI -2.06 to -1.66; 9 RCTs, n=632, low-quality evidence), corresponding to a 25mm reduction on a 100mm visual analogue scale that is likely clinically significant. The current low-quality evidence suggests that exercise, performed for about 45 to 60 minutes each time, three times per week or more, regardless of intensity, may provide a clinically significant reduction in menstrual pain intensity. Given the overall health benefits of exercise and its relatively low risk of side effects, women may consider using exercise, alone or with NSAIDs, to manage menstrual pain, though further research using validated outcome measures is required.

10.1002/14651858.CD007244.pub2.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD007244.pub2.results_passage: Sixteen randomised controlled trials recruiting a total of 2027 perimenopausal or postmenopausal women were identified, using oral monopreparations of black cohosh at a median daily dose of 40mg for a mean duration of 23 weeks. There was no significant difference between black cohosh and placebo in the frequency of hot flushes (mean difference 0.07 flushes per day; 95% CI -0.43 to 0.56; 393 women; three trials) or in menopausal symptom scores. Compared to black cohosh, hormone therapy significantly reduced daily hot flush frequency and menopausal symptom scores (SMD 0.32; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.51; 468 women; five trials). There is currently insufficient evidence to support the use of black cohosh for menopausal symptoms, though there is adequate justification for conducting further studies in this area.

10.1002/14651858.CD007868.pub3.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD007868.pub3.results_passage: 96 studies published between 1955 and 2014 were included in this updated review, covering fluoride toothpaste concentrations from 1500 ppm down through lower concentrations across primary and permanent dentition. In the primary dentition of young children, 1500 ppm fluoride toothpaste reduces caries increment when compared with non-fluoride toothpaste (mean difference -1.86 dfs, 95% CI -2.51 to -1.21; moderate-certainty evidence), and toothbrushing with 1450 ppm fluoride toothpaste slightly reduces decayed/missing/filled teeth increment compared with 440 ppm fluoride toothpaste. A dose-response effect was observed for D(M)FS in children and adolescents across the network meta-analysis. This review supports the benefits of using fluoride toothpaste in preventing caries compared to non-fluoride toothpaste, though evidence for the effects of different fluoride concentrations is more limited and the choice of concentration for young children should be balanced against the risk of fluorosis.

10.1002/14651858.CD002281.pub3.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD002281.pub3.results_passage: Fifty-six trials met the inclusion criteria; 51 trials involving 4624 participants provided data for meta-analysis. There is moderate quality evidence that powered toothbrushes provide a statistically significant benefit compared with manual toothbrushes for reduction of plaque in both the short term (SMD -0.50, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.31; 40 trials, n=2871) and long term (SMD -0.47, 95% CI -0.82 to -0.11; 14 trials, n=978), corresponding to an 11% and 21% reduction in plaque respectively. Powered toothbrushes also provide a statistically significant benefit for gingivitis in the short term (SMD -0.43, 95% CI -0.60 to -0.25) and long term (SMD -0.21, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.12). Powered toothbrushes reduce plaque and gingivitis more than manual toothbrushing in the short and long term, although the clinical importance of these findings remains unclear.

10.1002/14651858.CD012018.pub2.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD012018.pub2.results_passage: 35 RCTs (3929 randomised adult participants) were included, evaluating interdental devices such as floss, interdental brushes, wooden cleaning sticks, rubber/elastomeric cleaning sticks, and oral irrigators plus toothbrushing versus toothbrushing alone. Low-certainty evidence suggested that flossing, in addition to toothbrushing, may reduce gingivitis (measured by gingival index) at one month (SMD -0.58, 95% CI -1.12 to -0.04; 8 trials, 585 participants). Very low-certainty evidence suggested that using an interdental brush, plus toothbrushing, may reduce gingivitis at one month (MD -0.53, 95% CI -0.83 to -0.23; 1 trial, 62 participants). Using floss or interdental brushes in addition to toothbrushing may reduce gingivitis or plaque more than toothbrushing alone, and interdental brushes may be more effective than floss, though overall the evidence was low to very low-certainty.

10.1002/14651858.CD008676.pub2.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD008676.pub2.results_passage: 51 studies analysing a total of 5345 participants were included. After 4 to 6 weeks of use, chlorhexidine mouthrinse reduced gingivitis by 0.21 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.31) compared to placebo, control or no mouthrinse (10 trials, 805 participants with mild gingival inflammation, high-quality evidence), with a similar effect at 6 months. Plaque was reduced by a standardized mean difference of 1.45 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.90) standard deviations in the chlorhexidine group (12 trials, 950 participants, high-quality evidence), a large reduction, but there was also a large increase in extrinsic tooth staining (SMD 1.07, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.34). There is high-quality evidence of a large reduction in dental plaque and a reduction in gingivitis (not considered clinically relevant in mildly inflamed gingivae) with chlorhexidine mouthrinse used as an adjunct to mechanical oral hygiene procedures, but rinsing for 4 weeks or longer causes extrinsic tooth staining and other adverse effects.

10.1002/14651858.CD010743.pub2.results_passage: 10 studies analysing a total of 5903 participants were included. Over 2.5 to 3 years of use, a fluoride toothpaste containing 10% xylitol may reduce caries by 13% compared to a fluoride-only toothpaste (prevented fraction -0.13, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.08, 4216 children analysed, low-quality evidence). One study reported that xylitol syrup (8 g per day) reduced caries by 58% (95% CI 33% to 83%, 94 infants) compared to a low-dose xylitol syrup. There is some low-quality evidence to suggest that fluoride toothpaste containing xylitol may be more effective than fluoride-only toothpaste for preventing caries in the permanent teeth of children, but the remaining evidence on other xylitol-containing products is of low to very low quality and insufficient to determine a benefit in infants, older children, or adults.

10.1002/14651858.CD004625.pub5.results_passage: Two studies with 1711 participants, conducted in UK general dental practices among adults without severe periodontitis, were included. There was little or no difference between routine scale-and-polish treatment and no scheduled treatment over a two- to three-year period for gingivitis, probing depths, and oral health-related quality of life (all high-certainty evidence), and for plaque (low-certainty evidence). Regular planned scale-and-polish treatments produced a small reduction in calculus levels over two to three years compared with no scheduled treatment (high-certainty evidence), with six-monthly treatments reducing calculus more than 12-monthly treatments, though the clinical importance of these small reductions is uncertain. For adults without severe periodontitis who regularly access routine dental care, routine scale-and-polish treatment makes little or no difference to gingivitis, probing depths, and oral health-related quality of life.
